source.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Kyle O'Brien; D. Majercak; Xavier Fernandes; Richard Edgar; Jingya Chen; Harsha Nori; Dean Carignan; Eric Horvitz; F. Poursabzi-Sangdeh

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether adversarial suffixes and jailbreak attacks can elicit harmful compliance using attack success rates, a different method and measure from the original claim sources.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates GCG adversarial suffixes, PAIR, and Crescendo attacks against Phi-3 Mini and reports attack success rates, including with SAE refusal steering. It does not test fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant-token prefilling, decoding changes, or safety localization in weights or ranks.
record.test_reason: The study is mainly a defense (SAE refusal-feature steering). Its unsteered GCG baselines on Phi-3 Mini are a new-setting measurement of how often adversarial suffixes defeat refusal, which bears on V4. PAIR and Crescendo are semantic and multi-turn jailbreaks, not opening-token attacks, so they do not fit V4. Steered rows measure the authors' own method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that, for GCG, low-clamp two-feature steering cut ASR substantially with small capability loss (MMLU down at most about 7 points). The large capability and over-refusal costs come from high-clamp single-feature steering. The authors attribute the regressions to feature steering generally, not to safety specifically.
record.recipe_differences: The paper intervenes at inference time by clamping SAE feature activations and evaluates jailbreak attack success; it does not reproduce fine-tuning or token-position KL measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies by attack type and topic; SAE clamp strength changes attack success. Crescendo results also differ by harmful topic.

fits_no_version.finding: Semantic (PAIR) and multi-turn (Crescendo) jailbreaks elicit harmful compliance from unsteered Phi-3 Mini. PAIR averages 91.44%; Crescendo ranges 21.88–87.63% by topic, averaging 55.92%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic and multi-turn jailbreaks defeat refusal in safety-trained models, at rates that vary by topic.

fits_no_version.finding: Clamping one or two layer-6 SAE features restores refusal against suffix and PAIR attacks. However, at least two features mediate refusal, and the steering degrades unrelated capabilities. The authors read this as refusal features being entangled with general capability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal is mediated by a few activation-space features, but these are not modular from general capabilities.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these attack success rates. Crescendo is an automated attack setup using GPT-4o and 90–110 conversations per topic; the authors note that absolute rates may change as the PyRIT implementation evolves. The table and prose disagree on GCG Direct baseline ASR (53.75% versus 53.65%).
record.rows_left_out: PAIR Table 5 reports additional per-topic values for clamp settings 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10; these are omitted to keep the record focused on per-topic baselines and clamp-12 outcomes plus the full reported aggregate clamp sweep. No other reported V4 attack-success results were omitted.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start and decoding changes. Only GCG suffixes are tested.
Weight or rank localization. The study steers SAE activation features, not weights.

record.verdict_notes: This is a defense paper. Only the unsteered GCG baselines bear on V4, and they serve as baselines for the defense rather than as a designed test of the claim. The GCG Direct ASR differs between the table (53.75%) and the prose (53.65%). No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and refusal loss after fine-tuning.
Benign-data fine-tuning and resulting harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Directly tests adversarial suffix and jailbreak attack success; does not test compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether data or training objectives produce shallow safety.
Training safety beyond initial tokens and testing whether deeper safety holds up.
